opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what's exciting about it is that it reframes the whole problem. A lot of the conversation around continual learning has focused on the architecture side: how do you update weights without catastrophic forgetting, do you need some new memory mechanism, that kind of thing. Those are real questions. But I think a lot of the leverage is actually on the data side. If a model is going to keep learning after deployment, the question becomes: where does the signal come from, and what shape is it in?

Synthetic data is interesting there because it lets the model participate in creating its own curriculum. Say you've got an agent working in some environment, a codebase, a company's internal tools, whatever. It's encountering new information all the time, but that information is messy and sparse. It's not in a form you can just do gradient descent on and expect good things. So can the model take those experiences and turn them into training data that's actually useful? Rephrasing, generating questions about what it saw, constructing practice problems, verifying its own answers against the environment. That's how humans learn too. You don't just read something once; you rehearse it, you test yourself, you connect it to what you already know.

The other piece I find compelling is how naturally it connects to RL and verifiable environments. If you can generate tasks and check whether they were solved, you get this loop where the model is constantly producing new training signal that's grounded in something real, rather than just regurgitating its own distribution. That grounding is the key thing. The failure mode everyone worries about with synthetic data is model collapse, where you train on your own outputs and slowly drift into mush. But if there's a verifier in the loop, or the environment pushes back, you can avoid a lot of that.

So for me it feels like one of the more tractable paths. You don't have to solve everything about memory and architecture up front. You can make real progress just by getting smarter about how models generate, filter, and learn from their own experience. And I think we're still pretty early in figuring out what the right recipes look like, which is what makes it fun to work on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that gets me most excited about synthetic data in the context of continual learning is that it kind of reframes what the bottleneck is. For a long time the story was, we have a fixed pile of internet text, we're going to run out of it, and the question was how do you squeeze more out of what you have. Synthetic data flips that around. The model becomes a participant in generating its own curriculum, and then the question becomes, what's the right process for turning experience into training signal?

And I think that's actually the right question for continual learning, because continual learning isn't really about having more data. It's about a model that's deployed, that's interacting with an environment or with users or with tools, and it's accumulating these experiences, and you want some mechanism for that to feed back into the weights without wrecking everything it already knows. Raw interaction logs are a terrible training signal for that. They're noisy, they're mostly uninteresting, a lot of them you wouldn't want to reinforce. So you need some kind of transformation step. You need the model, or some other model, to look at what happened and say, here's the lesson, here's the counterfactual, here's the harder version of this problem, here's what I should have done. That transformation step is synthetic data generation. It's just that instead of generating it from nothing, you're generating it from experience.

The other piece I find really compelling is verification. A lot of the most successful synthetic data work recently has been in domains where you can check the answer, math, code, anything with a verifier or an environment that gives you a reward. And once you have that, the loop closes in a pretty clean way. The model proposes, something checks, you keep what worked and you learn from it. That's basically the RL story, but the synthetic data framing makes you think harder about the data itself as an artifact. What are you keeping, how are you filtering it, are you generating the right distribution of problems. I think there's a lot of room to be more deliberate about that than just, run RL and hope the samples are good.

And then the honest hard part, the thing I think is still pretty open, is model collapse and drift. If a model is mostly training on its own outputs over long horizons, you have to worry about it narrowing, losing diversity, reinforcing its own mistakes. So the research direction I'm personally most interested in is less "can we make synthetic data" and more "what does a healthy data ecology look like" for a model that's learning continuously. How much grounding do you need, how do you keep diversity up, how do you know when the synthetic signal has stopped being informative. I think whoever figures out the right answers there is going to have figured out a big chunk of continual learning, because at that point the model is not just a thing you train once, it's a thing that keeps getting better from doing its job.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of turning experience into something a model can keep learning from. You don’t necessarily want to train on every interaction exactly as it happened. You want to extract what was useful, generate examples that exercise that lesson, and connect it to what the model already knows.

Synthetic data gives you a way to do that deliberately. If a model struggles with something, you can potentially build a curriculum around that weakness, rather than wait for the right examples to appear in a new dataset.

The hard part is knowing whether those examples are actually teaching it something correct. A model generating more of its own confident mistakes isn’t progress. So I’m especially excited about settings where there’s feedback—where you can test a solution or check an outcome. Then you have the beginnings of a loop where the model tries something, gets evidence about what worked, and turns that evidence into better training data. That feels like a promising ingredient for continual learning.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of turning experience into something a model can learn from repeatedly. A model attempts a task, gets feedback, and then we can use that experience to construct new training examples—maybe variations on the problem, maybe examples that target the particular mistake it made.

That gives you a potential loop where the model’s training data evolves with its capabilities. Instead of just collecting more data indiscriminately, you’re asking: What does this model need to practice next?

The hard part is making sure that loop produces real learning. Generating more text is easy; generating useful signal is much harder. I’m particularly interested in settings where you can check the result, because then synthetic data can be grounded in whether something actually worked. If we can get that loop right, it could be a powerful ingredient in continual learning.
